item.title: Introducing the PowerPool Points Program
item.dc:creator: Mr FOS
item.content:encoded:
It’s an exciting time for our community, we’re thrilled to announce the launch of the PowerPool Points Program!

As protocol continues its journey towards automating AI Agents and DeFI, the next chapter begins: the Points. Instead of rewarding testnet participants, this rewards program is for everyone. Use the protocol, build integrations with AI, run Keepers — all of it will provide points to you.

It starts on January 27, 2025, 00:00 GMT.

Register here to start earning Points. The registration guide can be found in the PowerPool docs.

How it works

The Points Program is structured around epochs, each lasting precisely two weeks. During these epochs, Keepers and Job-owners can earn points by registering and executing Jobs within the PowerAgent across all supported networks. After each epoch, every user’s earned points will be calculated in a final leaderboard where rewards are automatically distributed.

The prize pool for each epoch is set at 20,000 CVP, and ALL participants receive their share based on the points accumulated throughout the epoch.

How to earn points

Keepers can accumulate points by executing transactions within the PowerAgent network. Each successful Job completion adds a specific number of points to your account. The exact point value is determined by the gas cost associated with the executed Job — meaning the more complex the Job, the greater the rewards!

Job-owners also benefit from this system; they earn points every time their Job is executed. We encourage everyone to delegate their web3 actions — routine or complex to PowerAgent.

The more transactions do you execute and the more gas is spent, the more points you earn

*Attention: The PowerPool team does not participate in the Points Program.

The Referral Program: you win, friends win

Note that the PowerPool Points Program includes a referral system. Each registered user receives a unique referral link to share with friends. Referrers will earn a bonus 15% of the points earned by their referees, while referees enjoy a 200-point welcome bonus upon registration and retain 100% of their earned points.

It pays to have on-chain friends.

See you in our socials and happy points farming!

Twitter | Discord | YouTube | Telegram | CMC Community | Debank | Medium

PowerPool Update — October 2024

Hello, PowerPool Community!

Welcome to the most recent update regarding PowerPool’s developments and achievements in the past month.

In this article, we will cover:

  1. PowerAgent V2: Network stats
  2. PowerAgent Code & UI changes
  3. R&D activities

Let’s explore this in detail!

PowerAgent V2: Network stats

To participate in the PowerAgent testnet, join the PowerPool Discord!

PowerAgent Code & UI Updates

Here is a list of code and UI updates that were done during the recent months. Note, that some of links point to private repos and later will have public access.

Contracts:
- We reworked the VRF architecture so that the call to fulfill random words is made from the agent to the VRFAgentCoordinator, not the VRFAgentConsumer;

- We reworked the contract deployment process by adding PPAgentV2VRFBased support, a script to generate JSON for verification, and a test to fulfill the resolver using the time machine.

- We added an agent to getRequestData and improved the agent repository for testing on the server.

- We investigated the bug: Blacklist on slashing error (SlashingNotInitiatedExecutionReverted), but it could not be reproduced.

- We added the deactivateJob method to the Agent Manager.

- We migrated the agent on Linea to the new consumer version.

- We developed a prototype version of the safety module.

- We tested the process of bridge-created sidechain token contracts and analyzed their requirements.

- We tested the CVP bridge locker across different networks.

- We deployed CVP and the bridge locker to the Base chain.

- We investigated the use of the Arbitrum native bridge for CVP.

Liquidation Protection Contracts:

- We conducted a test to measure gas expenses for executing protection with 1 and 2 tokens on the Gnosis chain.

- We made LP strategy ownership non-transferable.

- We added a MultiToken strategy.

- We adjusted baseToToken to better handle rounding errors.

- We included reservoir balance and approval checks in the resolver.

- We added a deployedStrategies mapping and a knownAddressRegistries list to the Factory.

- We deployed the LP strategy for tokens on Arbitrum and triggered HF bumps.

- We added some forked tests for the MultiToken strategy.

- We added more mocked tests for the MultiToken strategy, covering scenarios with zero balances and full allowances, using only the first token with sufficient balance, using the second token with sufficient balance while other tokens are unused or have zero allowance, and similarly testing the third token with varied balance and allowance conditions.

- We fixed issues with running forked tests.

- We implemented a restriction to prevent setting protection for zero tokens.

Power Agent Node (TS):

- We debugged the resolver’s success callback and fixed the issue where resolver callbacks were not performing any actions.

- We fixed the issue with the _onNewBlockCallback error: `Cannot convert undefined to a BigInt.`.

- We investigated the issue where the interval was attempting to execute twice, but we couldn’t reproduce it.

- We fixed the slashing issue on Arbitrum where the error ‘Cannot connect to WS: RangeError: Max payload size exceeded’ occurred.

- We fixed the _onNewBlockCallback error: ‘Cannot mix BigInt and other types, use explicit conversions,’ which caused a stack TypeError.

- We added logging to address the QueueEmitter.execute error.

- We fixed the Graph meta query error: `TypeError: Cannot convert null to a BigInt`.

- We investigated the issue with txExecutionFailed: insufficient funds for intrinsic transaction cost despite having a $10 balance on Arbitrum. The problem resolved itself.

- We fixed the slashing issue by updating queryJob for the Subquery data source.

- We investigated and fixed the issue where the Subgraph was 281,278 blocks behind on node startup.

- We configured node and Explorer tests to run in Docker with a PostgreSQL database to eliminate local environment issues and better align the test environment with production.

- We fixed the issue of excessive requests from the keeper causing RPC overload on Gnosis.

- We fixed the gas overestimation issue on Sepolia .

Power Agent Off-chain service (TS):

- We modified the VRFProofGenerator to use the consumer as the sender address in the preSeed.

- We updated the tests to use the VRFAgentConsumer as the job address.

- We started using a go-IPFS node to store and retrieve off-chain scripts ().

- We performed additional tests and debugged the off-chain service, fixing potential errors.

- We added a go-IPFS node to the Docker Compose configuration .

- We reworked scriptToExecute to fix the problem with the subquery on VRF.

- We fixed the IPFS connection to bootnodes and added limits for saving and downloading files.

- We made some updates to the off-chain service: deleted old scripts on startup and did some minor refactoring.

- We implemented a potential fix for the issue where the container couldn’t be killed, resulting in a zombie state.

- We fixed an issue in the off-chain service by correcting the scriptsToExecute path, which was causing a ‘Cannot find module’ error.

- We fixed an issue in the off-chain service where build script objects were empty on service startup.

- We fixed the issue of IPFS taking up too much space by resetting it every 24 hours.

- We investigated the issue of no polling resolvers after reconnection on Base, caused by server connection problems with the internet.

dApp:

- We created a Points Leaderboard page.

- We created a Points Referral page.

- We created Points Overview page.

- We created Points Account page.

- We added all necessary functionality to the overview and leaderboard pages and performed testing.

- We performed tests and fixed issues on the Referral page.

- We performed tests and fixed issues on the Points Account page.

- We finished the markup and logic for the Points Overview page.

- We finished the markup and logic for the Points Account page.

- We tested two Points epochs and implemented some fixes.

- We finished the markup and logic for the Points Referral page.

- We finished the markup and logic for the Points Leaderboard page.

- We fixed the referral link generation and copying functionality in the Overview page markup.

- We made adaptive design and markup fixes for the Points program pages.

- We added navigation to the Points Account page.

- We made some minor UI fixes after the review. [1][2]

- We fixed the issue with initContracts when using a referral link. The problem occurred when visiting the page via a referral link — if the wallet wasn’t connected, the issue could only be resolved by reloading the page.

- We conducted tests on the new keeper creation and registration in the Points system. [3][4]

- We added the job owner to the UI and tested it.

- We fixed bugs from the markup review, removed a deprecated button, and improved design system element.

- We added network information to the Points leaderboard.

- Following testing, we fixed points-related issues: corrected broken leaderboard rankings on page 2, addressed missing points earnings after multiple job executions, resolved an issue where users still saw epoch 2 in epoch 3, and clarified the registration reward row name to reduce user confusion.

- We redesigned the job creation page based on the new layout, simplified the interfaces, and updated the data input forms.

- We redesigned the agent list page by removing unnecessary elements and simplifying the interface. The page now consists of a single list of agents with collapsible elements, rather than a two-part layout. When creating keepers or jobs, the required agent will expand automatically.

- We redesigned the ‘All Keepers’ page based on the new layout, with a focus on improving the filtering system, as it occasionally malfunctioned after applying the agent filter.

- We redesigned the ‘All Jobs’ page based on the new layout. Additionally, we removed overly complex, separate forms for mobile devices; resizing the existing desktop elements now suffices for mobile compatibility.

- We prepared the Subquery infrastructure for new contracts on Linea and Arbitrum and integrated these contracts into the application’s UI. [5][6]

- We redesigned the ‘My Jobs’ page based on the new layout, with special attention to adding filtering similar to the ‘All Jobs’ page and limiting displayed jobs to the selected agent.

- We redesigned the ‘My Keepers’ page according to the new layout. Unlike the ‘All Keepers’ page, the list elements now include detailed information about each keeper.

- We redesigned the Explorer Keepers page, updating main elements such as search and replacing filtering elements with ones that follow the new design.

- We redesigned the Jobs page in the Explorer.

- We redesigned the Transactions page in the Explorer.

- We redesigned the Statistics page in the Explorer.

- We updated the agent picker UI to make it clearer which agent is selected. Displaying only the agent address was insufficient, so we added the agent name for better clarity.

- We added auto-selection of agents with existing keepers on the My Keepers page.

- We fixed an issue where the ‘Create Keeper’ button at the bottom was not working.

- We fixed an issue where keeperFrom and keeperTo fields were empty in the executions list.

- We added the Liquidation Protection app to the PowerPool dApp.

- We fixed an issue where jobs were not updating after release or balance withdrawal.

- We improved the ‘Next Execution’ logic to correct an issue where unassigned jobs were incorrectly displayed as ‘Already Executing’ in the UI.

- New feature: implemented a 30-second interval update for jobs with the status ‘Already Executing.’ While active, setInterval refreshes the job status every 30 seconds, updating the history to reflect new debit (execute) entries when the status changes.

- We investigated how the Arbitrum bridge affects the UI flow.

- We added off-chain resolver jobs to the job creation process.

- We reworked the Bridge UI to support any DeBridge network.

- We fixed an issue where the UI didn’t function correctly with different contracts on Linea and Arbitrum. [7][8]

Cross-chain DCA trading strategy dApp:

- We conducted a basic test of the DCA strategy;

- We migrated to a new version of Webpack to resolve Node-gyp failures on macOS. We also attempted to use a VM during the process.

Aave Liquidation protection dApp:

- We implemented Aave position fetching and added a link for creating positions in the protection app.

- We initialized the Liquidation Protection app, removing any unnecessary code from the PowerPool boilerplate. Although based on the PowerPool framework, this application will be significantly simpler, so eliminating redundant code was essential to streamline it for production.

- We created an interface for deploying smart contracts from the factory in the Liquidation Protection app.

- We added UI functionality for editing protection tokens, enabling users to remove and add tokens, change token order, and add any missing allowances from the contract creation phase.

- We added functionality to edit protection contract parameters, allowing users to modify the target and trigger health factors and deprecate the protection contract if needed.

- We updated the main protection UI by enhancing the protection indicator and adding a protection tokens list.

- We added functionality to accept job transfers and provide allowances for protection tokens after the protection contract is created.

UI/UX:

- We created a design template for the Safety module.

- We created a complete design for the ‘Liquidity Protection’ dApp.

- We created a complete design for the ‘Points’ section.

- We made changes to the header by adding a Points indicator.

- We added the agent name to the agent filter.

- We added an agent picker to the Explorer.

subQuery:

- We investigated the missing Keeper slashing information and fixed it by resyncing the Subquery.

- We investigated and fixed the issue where Subquery would randomly stop and not restart.

- We fixed the issue of the Polygon Subquery lagging by more than 200 blocks. This delay was critical for the ecosystem, as Polygon requires a 200-block wait to prevent forking before data retrieval. We reduced this delay to 20 blocks to improve responsiveness.

- We fixed an issue where the Subquery on Arbitrum production was failing due to the unfinalized-blocks option.

Explorer:

- We implemented basic referral logic in Explorer, with verification using Dune Analytics.

- We made several improvements to resolve the issue of Explorer not being up to date.

- We added epochs and points reporting to the Explorer.

- We added compensation and transaction fees to the transactions in the Explore.

- We added functionality to calculate points based on compensation and initialized API endpoints.

- We improved the backend for frontend integration and performed testing.

- We performed tests, fixed issues in the Explorer, and added rewards for users joining the Points program.

- We optimized the database by removing the ReferralInvited model, adding the ReferralAction model, and creating compensation actions in onTransactionReferral.

- We replaced transactions with referral actions in the Explorer and tested the account page list.

- We added leaderboard addresses, referralTotalPointsGave, and updated the referral epoch on new transactions.

- We updated pointsPerCompensationPerNetwork and tested two epochs in the Points Explorer.

- We created a snapshot for the previous epoch and improved the filtration process.

- We improved the referral points system by adding a database column to track how many points a referral has given to their referee. This value is fixed at the time of snapshots and is summed with previous amounts.

- We added safeExecute and a referral existence check, and renamed GlobalReferralEpoch. Middleware was implemented to prevent users from double or triple claiming points, addressing the previous issue where users could click twice and receive double rewards. This feature makes that no longer possible. Additionally, API security was improved, and the model was renamed.

- We added UserTotalReferralEpoch and middleware support to the worker’s endpoint. Previously, the middleware worked fine in the main thread but lacked support inside worker threads. This update adds middleware support for API requests within worker threads. Additionally, UserTotalReferralEpoch was introduced to sum up all user referral earnings per epoch.

- We conducted additional tests and improved the API for the UI.

- We updated the Points Explorer by setting a new configuration, resetting the database, and testing new values.

- We improved the creation of providers with a stable RPC URL in the Explorer.

- We fixed the retrieval of the job address from the execute txData.

- We added and tested jobOwner compensation points in the Explorer.

- We fixed the ‘undefined’ error when creating blacklist jobs. The issue was in the parseAndSetUnrecognizedErrorMessage function, which caused empty error messages in some cases.

- We debugged and fixed the issue with the user total epoch not updating in the leaderboard.

- We improved the /api/referral/users-epochs endpoint in the Explorer.

- We improved the Explorer to test the Points system, added environment variables, enhanced the configuration, and fixed the database schema to function in the new test environment.

- We created an automated test for the Points system, improved the Docker environment to execute tests, wrote a test to verify general values in the Points system, and resolved Docker bug docker/for-mac#6956.

- We addressed points issues reported by beta testers by improving RPC switching to more stable options, handling failed requests with automatic RPC switching, enhancing logging for RPC issues, fixing referral action constraints, refactoring API endpoint code, and updating the RPC endpoint list by removing unavailable endpoints and replacing them with active ones.

- We conducted automated tests and fixed bugs, including improving logging for unavailable providers, enforcing model conditions for tests, creating base method signatures if absent, changing epoch duration from one week to two, fixing total epoch updates, and correcting the recording of referralPointsAmount in the database.

- We debugged and fixed the issue with compensationPointsAmount not updating in the Points Explorer.

Landing page:

- We added Linea and Gnosis diagrams to the pie chart on the landing page.

- We added Polygon to the pie chart.

- We improved the landing page’s stability to ensure real-time project statistics load reliably, even on unstable internet connections.

Infrastructure:

- We launched an additional BASE node.

- We launched an additional OP node.

- We launched an additional Linea node.

- We launched an additional archive Ethereum node.

- We fixed an issue on the Gnosis node related to widespread block requests by configuring NGINX logging for JSON-RPC requests with IP addresses, reducing the maximum block query limit for eth_getLogs from 20K to 5K, and lowering the request timeout from 20s to 10s. No new issues have occurred.

- We updated the Arbitrum node to the latest version.

- We updated the Gnosis node to the latest version.

R&D activities

The PowerPool research team tracked all node activity, provided $CVP airdrops, tested all software updates & features mentioned above, and reported issues to the development team. One of the most important activities was testing the new points system, which is planned to be released soon, after closing the legacy one and distributing rewards to the legacy points owners.

item.title: The team statement following the CVP delisting from Binance
item.dc:creator: PowerPool
item.content:encoded:
Dear PowerPool community!

We deeply regret to inform you that $CVP, the PowerPool native token will be delisted from Binance on 26–08–2024 according to the official announcement.

We decided to make a team statement and provide detailed information to the PowerPool community regarding the recent delisting announcement.

Key takeaways:

  • This decision was completely unexpected for us, and Binance didn’t provide any information on the specific reasons or triggers that led to the $CVP delisting.
  • PowerPool has been building a protocol and community, delivering tech and marketing activities, including the Binance CVP Learn and Earn.
  • PowerPool team provided detailed reports on the development and other activities requested by the Binance post-listing team.
  • Binance does not provide feedback on the reports or any other activities reported, nor does it give any information related to the reason for inclusion in the Monitoring tag.
  • The team hasn’t sold any portion of the team token allocation yet (tokens were unlocked approximately a year ago)
  • $CVP is available on multiple CEXes (Gate, Mexc, etc) and Uniswap DEX

The team comments on $CVP delisting

For the PowerPool team, maintaining relationships with the Binance Post-Listing team was a top priority.

We delivered all requested information/updates/reports to Binance representatives on demand, sometimes pausing other activities to deliver ASAP. We did it because the Binance listing is very important for the $CVP liquidity and community convenience.

The Binance Post-Listing team was informed in detail about our technical, marketing, event activities, community metrics, testnets, AMAs, and everything else that is being done. When $CVP got a monitoring tag, we tried to get some information about the reasons and understand what should be improved; for this purpose, we spent about 1.5 months setting up the call with someone from Binance Post-Listing to understand what we could do.

Unfortunately, the call was never organized under the pretext of various reasons communicated to us by the post-listing team. From our side, we made a lot of efforts, reminding and asking about the possibility of a call; in the end, we were ignored.

We tried to do our best from all sides:
- We deployed PowerPool on 6 networks, onboarded Keeper Nodes, and projects building on top of PowerPool via the grants program run in collaboration with Gitcoin
- We updated the narrative and focused on AI; we won a hackathon to demonstrate that PowerPool’s AI vision isn’t just a buzzword (unlike some other projects) but an actual use case
- We created and partly executed a vast marketing plan, co-hosted an ETHCC side event with top-tier projects and planned to proceed with it in Seoul/Singapore, and got publications in media outlets like Coindesk

Most importantly, we demonstrated that decentralized transaction automation works, and our next step was to extend this vision to all major EVM ecosystems and AI projects operating within them.

We are a small, independent project without VC funding. We tried to leverage novel technology and community support to grow and deliver a useful Web3 product that Defi and web3-focused AI protocols need.

We would also like to specifically mention that the team did not sell team tokens that were fully unlocked more than a year ago.

Now, with all our innovation and vision, we didn’t meet Binance’s requirements.

Unfortunately, we don’t understand what particular requirements we didn’t meet (since the trading volumes were quite good for our market cap). Anyway, we don’t have answers and probably will never get them.

Today, the delisting is giving us very negative impressions of the overall brand and project image, which is unrelated to our tech or product quality.

PowerPool is a decentralized protocol whose operation doesn’t depend on CEX listings. The $CVP token remains available for the community on CEXes like MEXC, Gate, HTX, WhiteBit; and at Uniswap DEX.

The future steps and how the community can support $CVP after Binance delisting

It is disappointing that such decisions of big centralized corporations enormously influence independent community-driven projects.

The widespread vision is that delisting from Binance means the project is doomed. Completely dead. However, is this true?
When thousands have been developing BTC and ETH and believe in true decentralization, did we all expect such a future as it is now?

The core idea of web3 is self-sovereignty and independence from large institutions. Code doesn’t need permission from listing managers to operate, and mechanism design works regardless of anyone’s opinion.

Today, we are calling on the community to help us prove that decentralization works. Let’s make it great again!

Today, PowerPool has:

  1. The codebase that works (already deployed/being tested on various networks)
  2. Roadmap with already allocated funds for a future expansion
  3. The $CVP token is still liquid (other CEXes/DEXes), which means that there is liquidity and funding
  4. The loyal community of node runners
  5. Twitter has a good Twitterscore and many top web3 accounts subscribed.

What we expect from the community:

  1. We need your proposals on how to expand the project further.
    We need your ideas and energy to amplify PowerPool’s presence in various ecosystems. We have many tokens allocated to EVM chains. These tokens are valuable and ready to accelerate the protocol’s growth.
  2. For example, let’s brainstorm together about how to get more nodes and Job Owners and distribute tokens to the community as rewards.
    You, as a community member, can get involved today.
  3. We kindly ask our community to spread the word: make a post with your view on the situation and ideas on how to move forward

We are happy to remain transparent and accessible for any concerns or questions from the community.

PowerPool Monthly Update — 29 July 2024

It is time to share our traditional monthly update with the PowerPool Community!

In this article, we will cover:

  1. PowerPool marketing activity
  2. PowerAgent V2: the network stats
  3. PowerAgent Code & UI changes
  4. R&D results

PowerPool marketing activities

Recently, PowerPool updated its narrative, laser-focusing on web3 sectors with the biggest potential for increasing automation adoption: web3-focused AI Agents and Defi applications on major L2s.

We delivered extensive activities before and during the ETHCC conference to raise awareness of project updates. Let’s dig into the results!

PowerPool new vision showcased at the Hack Seasons event

PowerPool co-hosted the Hack Seasons, one of the major side events during the ETHCC week. The lineup included the biggest projects in the Ethereum ecosystem and beyond such as EigenLayer, Linea, Scroll, StarkNet, and many more:

PowerPool performed three main activities during the event:

  1. Sharing the information, merch, and performing BD activities with projects on the dedicated PowerPool Booth
  2. Vasily Sumanov, a Head of Research, delivered a talk on PowerPool’s new vision, tech, and value proposition for AI Agents and L2s
  3. Vasily also participated in a panel discussion with other industry experts.

We’ve had a lot of discussions with projects regarding using PowerPool automation in Defi and AI. The first public follow-up activity is scheduled as an AMA with 0G Labs, POND, GaiaNet, IoTeX, and Zk.Link devoted to AI-powered optimization of user stories in web3.

PowerPool published and distributed the new vision via media outlets

The new PowerPool vision focused on executing transactions for AI Agents and Defi projects on leading L2s was published to the community and distributed to several media outlets:

  1. The original PowerPool 2.0 medium post
  2. Coindesk press release
  3. Decrypt press release
  4. Mpost article

Other media publications related to PowerPool

  1. The updated 2024 Roadmap article
  2. The dAGI hackathon (POND bounty) winning article
  3. Articles mentioning PowerPool activities during the Hack Seasons [1],[2],[3]

PowerAgent network stats

The overall PowerPool network stats are presented below:

Stats for networks where PowerPool is deployed can be tracked in our Dashboard.

To participate in the PowerAgent testnet and earn rewards join the PowerPool Discord!

PowerAgent Code & UI changes

Here we share a list of code and UI updates that were done during the recent month. Note, that some of links belong to private repos and later will have public access.

Contracts:

  • We made some fixes to the VRFAgentConsumer deployment and deployed a Hardhat script to track the slasher ID for debugging purposes (https://github.com/powerpool-finance/powerpool-agent-v2-dev/commit/4e5d64a20864b08679529e52db6ae55ba75cf6e1).
  • We deployed a VRF Power Agent on the Gnosis chain for testing purposes (https://github.com/powerpool-finance/powerpool-agent-v2-node/pull/110/files)
  • We wrote a test for two VRFAgentConsumer contracts registered in the VRFCoordinator (powerpool-finance/powerpool-agent-v2@c6dadb8)
  • We changed the Power Agent contract code to use tstore and tload for execution lock instead of the minKeeperCVP variable and EXECUTION_IS_LOCKED_FLAG (powerpool-finance/powerpool-agent-v2@875c6cb)
  • We deployed and upgraded a new Power Agent implementation on Arbitrum, supporting tstore and tload for execution lock.(https://arbiscan.io/tx/0xa2dde767910baea0a3d4d730697a6e6e3b2e67a579a86c65a1cc10c935e2a50a)
  • We added the updateJob() function to the VRFAgentManager contract (powerpool-finance/powerpool-agent-v2@b8ca1a5)
  • We fixed some tests for the two VRFConsumers (powerpool-finance/powerpool-agent-v2@7a1d0b0 and powerpool-finance/powerpool-agent-v2@455c0a9)
  • We modified VRF-related contracts and tests, including changing visibility of variables, updating function signatures, improving request handling, and ensuring proper fulfillment of randomness requests (powerpool-finance/powerpool-agent-v2@b371fdf)
  • We separated the setup of vrfJobKey and autoDepositJobKey into separate functions, moving them out of setVrfConfig() and setAutoDepositConfig() (powerpool-finance/powerpool-agent-v2@546bec3)
  • We created a script to generate Standard Solidity Input JSON files for each contract, remove unnecessary contract references to reduce their size, and save the cleaned files for successful Etherscan verification (https://github.com/powerpool-finance/powerpool-agent-v2-dev/commit/d1967254449d64a9a4b2c22e4a8a8bbd6edfc101)

  • We deployed and migrated to a new version of AgentManager (https://arbiscan.io/txs?a=0x29BfF390FC12C900Aaf0F2e51C06675Df691337a)
  • We reworked getBalanceRequiredToDeposit() and migrateFromOldManager() functions in the AgentManager contract (https://github.com/powerpool-finance/powerpool-agent-v2/pull/26/files#diff-8ebf3fe667595830c2389c4ab8d96cc3cba7de5f76f9732096cc345572bba60aL144)
  • We made Power Agent V2 compatible with the Shanghai hardfork (https://github.com/powerpool-finance/powerpool-agent-v2/pull/27/files)
  • We deployed Power Agent V2 on Linea and conducted initial testing (add linea network constants powerpool-finance/powerpool-agent-v2-node#115)
  • We added PowerAgentBased support (https://github.com/powerpool-finance/powerpool-agent-v2-dev/commit/c3fadfe957aa383cb4a6be17478d962813e1ad42)
  • We changed the Solidity version and inheritance to improve manual verification (https://github.com/powerpool-finance/powerpool-agent-v2/pull/28/files).
  • We made some test deployments in experiments for Linea, Optimism, Scroll, Blast, and zkSync to check how block.prevrandao works and to identify any potential issues with Power Agent deployment.
  • We developed the initial contract for the liquidation protection strategy for AAVE (https://github.com/powerpool-finance/powerpool-agent-v2-apps-dev/blob/main/aave3-hf-monitor/Strategy.sol)

Power Agent Node (TS):

  • We fixed the error _onNewBlockCallback error: Cannot read properties of undefined (reading ‘sendBlockDelayLog’) that occurred when the Power Agent Node started after Keeper registration (https://github.com/powerpool-finance/powerpool-agent-v2-node/pull/108/files).

item.title: Exploring the PowerPool ecosystem: Ethereum, Gnosis, and Arbitrum
item.dc:creator: PowerPool
item.content:encoded:
PowerPool is a DePIN layer for executing transactions for Defi and AI protocols based on on-chain and off-chain triggers.

The main focus for PowerPool expansion are L2s with low gas fees, high TVL, and extensive user base. Recently, PowerPool DAO approved the proposal for L2s expansion and rewards focused on rollups, most demanded by Defi users and capital owners.

Transactions, automatically executed by PowerPool bring more value to users, AI Agents, and rollups themselves since it allows to generate more transaction fees.

The PowerPool ecosystem is growing rapidly as more chains and integrations are added:

In this article, we will provide a brief overview of the PowerPool ecosystem on Ethereum, Gnosis, and Arbitrum. Statistics for all chains are available in the Mulichain Dashboard.

Ethereum

Currently SupremeDAO is the main member of the PowerPool ecosystem on Ethereum. They received a PowerPool DAO grant for automated yield strategy development focused on ETH yield generation. The first strategy launched on the mainnet is the Genesis Strategy, initially released in test mode.

SupremeDAO provides a DeFi protocol aimed at offering transparent, community-driven, high-yield opportunities. They aim to simplify interactions with DeFi protocols and maximize returns through one-click access to automated multi-protocol strategies for safe and transparent high yield.

The full version of the algorithm specification is presented below:

  • Initially, the CDP on crvUSD.curve.fi is opened against the wstETH collateral and crvUSD is borrowed.
  • Next, crvUSD is swapped for USDC on Curve.
  • Then, liquidity is provided to the D2D/USDC pool on Balancer. The received LP tokens of the pool are staked on Aura.finance and generate yield from swap fees, plus AURA and BAL token rewards.
  • A share of the rewards is used to bribe the pool rewards via the Paladin protocol.
  • All rewards are swapped to wstETH and used to increase the initially deposited collateral, which is also the user’s capital, so rewards are directly compounded.

One important aspect of this algorithm is that it protects the position from liquidation risks. It regularly checks the CDP’s collateral health ratio, maintaining it above 30%. If the ratio drops below this threshold, farmed CRV tokens are automatically sold to purchase crvUSD and increase the health ratio.

Learn more about SupremeDAO project from their grant application, interview, and AMA.

Gnosis

Powerpool stats on Gnosis:

Gnosis was the first mainnet deployment for PowerPool. Since it is a low-fee chain, it suits great for automation in various ways, with more than 100 active Jobs launched.

One of the ecosystem partners using PowerPool for automation on Gnosis is Breadchain. Breadchain is a post-capitalist community of blockchain projects and protocols aimed at transparent public goods funding. PowerPool provides them with automatic funding for projects based on their governance decisions.

Breadchain is also a member of our Builder Grants program, which they achieved by incorporating decentralized and reliable automation into their projects.

Learn more about Breadchain project from their grant application, interview, and AMA.

Discussing other automation applications, it’s essential to highlight validators’ rewards claiming Jobs. These Jobs efficiently automate GNO rewards claims and seamlessly swap them for stablecoins or other assets.

Read more details here and check out the example of a job.

Arbitrum

On Arbitrum, PowerPool currently automates operations for two protocols: Gearbox and Partitura. These automated processes enhance efficiency by managing complex tasks that would otherwise require significant manual intervention.

Partitura is a protocol that simplifies Web3 by offering Account Abstraction solutions, Automated Workflows, and Intent-driven AI. It allows users to create custom flows — a sequence of automated and bundled transactions:

Partitura created an integration of Safe’s account abstraction for PowerPool and also PowerPool DCA template. The project focuses on using PowerPool automation as an ecosystem infrastructure service for future products.

Gearbox is a protocol offering leveraged farming services, including leveraged points farming in popular protocols. PowerPool team found that rewards refilling for Gauge on Arbitrum could be automated, explored the Gearbox design, and created a Job that refills the Gauge with rewards. item.title: The “AI Hands” created by PowerPool won the POND track on the dAGI hackathon
item.dc:creator: PowerPool
item.content:encoded:
As we build the PowerPool DePIN layer for automation, we’ve noticed that more and more AI Agents dedicated to operating in Web3 are being released. These AI agents use on-chain and off-chain information to make decisions that should be implemented as a state update in some contracts. Examples of such decisions include trading and using various Defi strategies.

However, by default, AI agents cannot execute their decisions as transactions. This is simply not their core business. Some protocols that build AI agents have added an option to run or use bots provided by the protocol to implement decisions.

To highlight this issue, the PowerPool team members created the “AI Hands” project and presented an effective solution to the AI transaction execution challenge. The solution earned a bounty at the POND track during the dAGI hackathon, showcasing traction and receiving positive feedback from AI developers and judges.

This article will provide details of this solution and further development plans.

The AI Hands by PowerPool

AI Hands executes transactions on behalf of AI Agent users. We built it on top of POND, a protocol focused on providing trading decisions to its users based on cluster analysis of on-chain data.

The AI Hands is an off-chain resolver built on top of the PowerPool Keeper network. It listens to the POND API and executes transactions on behalf of the trading agent user when certain conditions are met.

The algorithm has a single decision resolver function and utilizes PowerPool’s Keeper network. It begins by calling the POND API to obtain model metrics. Trend accuracy is chosen as the target metric because the hourly forecast interval allows for linear approximation.

A typical off-chain resolver in PowerPool works as follows:

The algorithm includes safeguards to ensure the reliability of its decisions. If the accuracy of the current model falls below a certain threshold, the results are discarded and the execution instance is terminated. Conversely, if the accuracy exceeds the threshold, the POND API is called again to obtain predictions for the unstable token in the pair and the current price.

To further refine the decision process, the algorithm evaluates the predicted change of the unstable token in relative units. If this change falls below a user-defined threshold, the results are discarded again, as minimal changes may not justify the risk or cost associated with a swap.

Conclusions and Future Plans

The execution of AI-generated transactions is an emerging market with huge growth potential.

Use cases include AI-resolved intents, defi strategies, trading strategies, and many more. We plan to integrate POND and provide its users with an easy onboarding option to outsource transaction execution to PowerPool. Other protocols, especially intent-based, will follow, enriching the PowerPool ecosystem with a set of use cases and templates that provide users with a one-click execution of decisions generated by AI agents.

item.title: Powerpool 2.0: capturing the AI agents market
item.dc:creator: Mr FOS
item.content:encoded:
AI market needs

With new AI programs like Google’s Bard and OpenAI’s ChatGPT, the AI market is set to grow massively. According to the latest stats, it’s predicted to soar from $40 billion, which was reached in 2022, up to $1.3 trillion in the next decade. The growth might happen at a rate of 42% per year, mainly because of the infrastructure for training these AI systems in the short-term period. Later, growth could be noticed in spheres such as language models, digital ads, special software, and services.

Additionally, a growing demand for AI products could bring an extra $280 billion in software sales due to specialized assistants, new infrastructure products, and copilots that make coding faster. Big companies like Amazon WebServices, Microsoft, Google, and Nvidiacan receive the highest benefits as more tasks are transferred to the public cloud.

Source: https://www.bloomberg.com/company/press/generative-ai-to-become-a-1-3-trillion-market-by-2032-research-finds/

The AI segment has received a lot of attention. AI agents supply users with various services, such as generating new data (content) and making decisions based on user requests. To provide such services, AI agents must be pre-trained on existing data.

AI agents automate time-consuming processes that previously required a lot of human intelligence and time. For example, content creation, business decision-making, or scientific applications such as searching for new molecules or drugs in medicine.

AI agents are trained and applied in Web3. They demonstrate promising capabilities in processing off-chain and on-chain data for automatic trading strategies and yield generation. and utilize dApps and protocols more intelligently and efficiently.

The main result provided by AI agents is the decision on specific on-chain actions generated by processing available on-chain data. However, only when the transaction triggered by AI as a result of its operation added to the block is the decision made by the AI agent created on-chain.

In this article, we share an update on PowerPool’s vision, which is focused on providing the backbone for the operation of Web3-focused AI agents. This addition to the existing PowerPool expansion strategy targeting retail users and Defi protocols is a major step forward.

What is PowerPool 2.0?

PowerPool consistently identifies the ongoing challenges in the Web3 market. It offers effective solutions while listening to project needs and the broader community. As the market evolves, PowerPool strives to keep pace.

In 2020, PowerPool was among the first to introduce functioning DeFi indices and meta-governance concepts. Thanks to our DAO and community members, PowerPool evolved into a decentralized network of Keeper-executors for flexible DeFi strategies.

Currently, various networks offer resources for on-chain and off-chain model training. Converting AI-created on-chain actions (triggers) into the updated state according to the AI agent’s decision requires running its Keepers/Bots executing trigger-based transactions.

Considering our experience as a DePIN, we decided to enhance the capabilities of PowerPool Keepers and to streamline the automation of AI agents’ decision execution. The main idea is to utilize PowerPool as an “execution hand” for advanced transaction execution based on AI queries and generated triggers.

PowerPool network as a tool for implementing AI decisions on-chain

PowerPool develops and operates as a DePIN network of Keeper bots. The network’s main service is the automatic execution of on-chain transactions based on on-chain and off-chain triggers.

The service provided by the PowerPool network is Transaction Execution as a Service. It executes transactions and their sequences (referred to as Jobs and flows thereafter) according to the execution algorithms. Applied to the Web3 AI agents sector, PowerPool can be an essential tool supplementing the operation of AI agents on-chain.

Let’s check out theAI agent (Web2 vs Web3) operational cycle:

Web2:

Pre-Training -> Receiving user’s prompt -> generating output -> implementing output and delivering the final result to the user (provide content/data to user or use the API to make some action on the Internet such as sending e-mail).

Web3:

Pre-Training (often on on-chain data) -> Receiving user’s prompt -> generating output (what exactly to do on-chain, e.g., buy token or stake token in a specific contract) -> [!] output implementation and delivering the final result as a state update in the blockchain network (executed transaction on behalf of the user).

AI agents operate off-chain and cannot execute transactions themselves. The output implementation phase mentioned above requires the generation and execution of transactions on-chain. These AI agent protocols must be augmented with a special infrastructure that includes a keeper bot to technically execute transactions on-chain, execution algorithms, RPC on each supported chain, and MEV protection if needed.

There are several options for AI protocol designers to make the output implementation phase possible:

  1. Create their own protocol-specific centralized Bots to execute transactions on behalf of AI models launched by users.
  2. Build their decentralized infrastructure (a Keeper bot network) with cryptoeconomic security mechanisms and other necessary features.
  3. Outsource the transaction execution part of the AI agent cycle to the dedicated DePIN network of Keeper bots, entirely focused on transaction execution

Considering the options above, there are the following comments:

  1. Centralized bot infrastructure creates a single point of failure. It exposes the AI protocol to a significant risk of failed executions, leading to user losses and other problems.
  2. A decentralized Keeper bot infrastructure is not a core business for the AI agent protocols. However, some early projects have followed this path, creating their own keeper networks for just one protocol. However, it is fundamentally out of scope for most AI protocols since building and running a properly decentralized network on different chains takes a lot of time and effort. It does not make sense to reinvent the wheel when there are networks on the market that are dedicated to solving the problem of automated transaction execution.
  3. Outsourcing transactions to existing DePIN Keeper networks and offering Transaction Execution as a Service seems preferable, as it eliminates the need to operate and maintain a dedicated infrastructure. In turn, it allows new AI agent models to be deployed as soon as they are developed, significantly reducing the time required for mainnet on-chain testing and overall go-to-market.

The design of the PowerPool network allows the creation of off-chain triggers that retrieve required data by making API calls and initiating job execution. This unlocks a huge opportunity to execute transactions on behalf of AI agents according to their decision-making strategies.

PowerPool has the following advantages to share with AI agents protocols and their users:

1. It offers transaction execution services with a wide range of conditions (on-demand execution or any kind of strategy) using the AI agents’ protocol API.

It means easy onboarding. So, the protocol that intends to use PowerPool to propagate AI agents’ actions on-chain doesn’t need to develop something specific.

2. It is executed by the decentralized and permissionless network built focusing on robustness and autonomous operation.

It means reliability and simplicity — the Tx execution is secured by PowerPool’s diversified Keepers’ set coordinated by staking/slashing mechanics and not related to the AI agents protocol itself. The AI agents’ protocol doesn’t need to run or maintain any kind of specific infrastructure. It works simply out of the box.

Used for AI transaction execution, PowerPool acts as a DePIN layer for AI agent protocols. By providing reliable and cost-effective propagation of off-chain AI decisions to on-chain state updates, PowerPool enhances its value and user experience.

As stated by Vasily Sumanov, Head of Research at PowerPool:

“Our main goal is to facilitate the practical usage of AI Agents in Web3 by providing reliable infrastructure for AI operations and streamlining the user experience for AI strategy creators.

The expansion of the Web3-focused AI segment, coupled with the essential requirement to execute AI operations on blockchain networks, creates a substantial growth opportunity for PowerPool.

The influence of the new AI-focused vision on PowerPool protocol value

The PowerPool protocol’s ability to create value for users, node runners, and the community is tied to the extent of the market it can capture by executing transactions and strategies on behalf of users, including AI agents. This layer is a critical factor in facilitating user interactions with Web3 protocols. As PowerPool generates and completes transactions, node runners generate more fees, which in turn enhances the overall value of the protocol.

“PowerPool is the ultimate transaction growth layer for networks with low transaction fees, large user bases, and substantial liquidity. It unlocks new use cases on top of automated strategies and AI decision implementation, increasing the number of transactions and users’ convenience.”

The most recent DAO proposal focused on future L2 deployments and strategies to expand the user base on these chains.

By expanding its vision and focus to become an infrastructure layer for Web3-focused AI agent protocols, PowerPool greatly expands the potential number of transaction executions performed by PowerPool keepers.

The key factors of transaction executions within PowerPool:

  1. The number of L1/L2 chains where PowerPool is deployed and operating
  2. The number of customers on specific L1/L2 chains:

2.1. The number of third-party protocols using PowerPool.

2.2. The number of UI/UX integrated PowerPool Template Jobs. It, in turn, requires integration with UI/UX, Template Job development, and many more.

2.3. The number of AI agents that are used for on-chain actions via PowerPool transaction execution.

3. An incentive multiplicator (points) is applied to a particular L1/L2 chain, UI/UX, or AI agent protocol. The multiplicator means the difference in users’ execution activity in case of points provided for a particular L2/UI/AI vs. no rewards at all.

The template metrics are presented below on the example of DCA (Dollar Cost Average) automated strategy:

  1. The number of supported networks;
  2. The number of unique DCA Jobs launched by users;
  3. The total number of transactions;
  4. The total TVL deployed by users to launch DCA Strategies.

AI agents can potentially generate a lot of demand for transaction execution without the need to develop a specific product UI or perform complicated integrations, as they work on top of API calls. Given the projected growth of the AI sector in Web3, there is a huge opportunity to capture a share of this growth as an infrastructure network focused on this sector.

So, the PowerPool becomes a kind of proxy network serving the Web3 AI market:

  1. The PowerPool Keepers will capture a share of all gas fees paid by AI agents for their on-chain transactions since they receive an execution fee.
    It makes running a PowerPool Keeper an attractive opportunity since it directly allows one to earn fees from the growing Web3 AI sector. In turn, this leads to the growth of the PowerPool network signers’ set, overall robustness, decentralization, and level of the network crypto economic security (as a result of the greater total size of $CVP stakes).
  2. The $CVP token will capture value from multiple AI protocols simultaneously, acting as a kind of a (meta)proxy token for the AI agents market as more Web3 AI agent protocols (or their users) utilize PowerPool. The value captured by $CVP staking increases since it captures the fee stream from all executions for AI-related projects and operations.

AI trading models are a significant subdivision of AI services currently hosting projects in the devnet/testnet/mainnet phases. This sector is evidently necessary for transaction execution. The first protocol we’re considering to demonstrate PowerPool’s automation layer is POND. This protocol emphasizes cluster on-chain analysis, allowing users to create their own AI agents to oversee on-chain trading strategies.

PowerPool Monthly Update — 25 June 2024

Hello, PowerPool Community!

We are excited to present an overview of PowerPool’s recent updates and accomplishments over the past month.

In this article, we will cover:

  1. Updated PowerPool treasury allocations
  2. PowerAgent V2: Network stats
  3. PowerAgent Code & UI changes
  4. R&D results

Let’s dive into the details!

Updated PowerPool treasury allocations

The PowerPool DAO has recently approved a new structure to the Treasury allocation.

According to Proposal 65, the previously unallocated 28.8M $CVP will be transferred to new multi-sig wallets, each dedicated to fund specific growth activities. The new Treasury allocation includes Marketing, PowerPool Points, and a set of allocations dedicated to growing protocol brand and user base on emerging L2s:

  • Ecosystem Fund aimed at ecosystem growth, DAO expenses, rewarding contributors, etc. (~9.45M $CVP remaining)
  • PowerPool Points program focused on user acquisition on various chains (5M $CVP)
  • Marketing activities for growing brand awareness (4M $CVP)
  • Arbitrum growth activities (1.5M $CVP)
  • Optimism growth activities (1.5M $CVP)
  • Polygon growth activities (1.5M $CVP)
  • Base growth activities (1.5M $CVP)
  • Linea growth activities (1.5M $CVP)
  • Blast growth activities (1.5M $CVP)
  • Gnosis growth activities (1M $CVP)
  • Future L2s funding reserved for expansion onto other L2s (8M $CVP)
  • Unallocated funds reserved for funding other activities (1.83M $CVP remaining)

PowerAgent V2: Network stats

To participate in the PowerAgent testnet, join the PowerPool Discord!

PowerAgent Code & UI Updates

Contracts

  • We developed a special contract for Power Agent VRF implementation called VRFAgentManager. Its basic functionality includes handling all Power Agent owner’s functions, automatically withdrawing protocol fees, and replenishing Job balances for VRF executions.
  • We updated the implementations for Power Agent contracts on Ethereum, Polygon, and Sepolia to support the callResolverBeforeExecute_ flag.
  • We updated some Power Agent tests to support the latest VRF updates.
  • We deployed additional instances of Power Agent contracts on Arbitrum and Gnosis Chain to facilitate simpler internal testing.
  • We reworked the VRFAgentManager contract to support separate automatic balance replenishment for VRF execution and job balance monitoring.
  • We changed the fixed reward rate for Power Agent compensations to make it more effective with rollups.
  • We deployed the PowerAgent contract and token on BASE.
  • We added backward compatibility for the Power Agent VRF coordinator to support Chainlink VRF.
  • We made some improvements and added additional tests for the VRFAgentManager.
  • We developed a separate VRFConsumer factory, improved createConsumer, and deployed and tested the new version on Arbitrum.
  • We updated the Power Agent ABI in the Power Agent node to reflect the latest changes for VRF support.
  • We improved registerAutoDepositJob and added assignKeeperToAutoDepositJob in VRFAgentManager.
  • We reworked VRFAgentConsumer to use ChainSpecificUtil and eliminated the separate factory for Arbitrum.
  • We deployed the new VRF PowerAgent on Arbitrum.
  • We conducted tests on Arbitrum and improved VRFAgentConsumer.
  • We migrated from OpenZeppelin libraries to optimize the Power Agent size.
  • We identified and fixed an issue with double sending transactions containing random numbers.
  • We improved PowerAgent to better handle off-chain resolver return checks.
  • We adjusted the multiplier for fixed rewards.
  • We made some improvements to VRFAgentManager.
  • In VRFAgentManager, we improved functionality to automatically assign a Keeper to a VRF Job if it was unassigned during the ‘Automatic deposit’ Job execution.
  • In VRFAgentConsumer, we fixed an issue with submitting random numbers on the requested block.
  • In VRFAgentConsumer, we decided to use block.number instead of a rollup-specific method to request native blocks for random number requests and submissions.
  • We deployed the VRF implementation* of PowerAgent on Arbitrum.
  • We added the NODE_API_PORT and OFFCHAIN_API_PORT environment variables to the Docker Compose file.
  • We added VRFAgentCoordinator support in VRFAgentManager and moved structs from VRF to VRFAgentCoordinatorInterface.
  • We moved the job keys setup from config setters to separate setters in VRFAgentManager.

Power Agent Node (TS)

  • We fixed the API endpoints for hashing functions and removed some excess dependencies.
  • We completely reworked the PowerAgent node configuration override using environment variables based on a string template approach, providing greater flexibility.
  • We added BASE network support to the Power Agent node.
  • We added multicall support for the BASE network.
  • We performed testing for Power Agent VRF, cleared unused code, and refactored the start script.
  • We moved the Offchain service to the root, performed tests, and made fixes.
  • We fixed the websocket provider to facilitate testing.
  • We fixed* the offchain Docker environment and cleared some code.
  • We updated* some dependencies in the tests and fixed mockBlockEmit.
  • We updated callResolversAndTriggerCallbacks to use offchainResolverPending, preventing double calls.
  • We wrapped the timeout with a debounce in _onNewBlockCallback.
  • We added failedIntervalEstimationsInARow to prevent self-unassignment after a single failed estimation.
  • We updated* the ABI in the VRFProofGenerator script and optimized its size.
  • We fixed writeVersionData.ts and added Git support to the Dockerfile.
  • We added RemoveJobFromBlacklist to the Power Agent configuration update.
  • We handled the provider.getLogs error when making requests to a node with restrictions.
  • We debugged* the VRFProofGenerator script, caught errors, and identified the causes.
  • We updated* dependencies in the Power Agent Node tests and tested offchainResolverPending.
  • We added the offchain service to the docker-compose file.
  • We fixed the offchain service environment.
  • We changed the resolver period call to custom.
  • We made an override for base fee and priority fee.
  • We fixed an issue with timers when transaction estimation failed several times in a row.
  • We fixed a problem where, in the mode where the Power Agent Node requested blocks directly, events were missed.
  • We fixed an error where an event was missing.

dApp

  • We completely reworked the details page in the Pools section.
  • We fixed the issue where the max fee per gas was less than the block base fee.
  • We fixed the issue with filters on the All Jobs page.
  • We fixed the incorrect timestamps in the event explorer.
  • We implemented a design system in the dApp.
  • We implemented a new menu appearance.
  • We added test agents for Gnosis and Arbitrum.
  • We fixed the hardcoded recommended gas price for Arbitrum.
  • We added the BASE network.
  • We removed unused code, including the Analytics page, Oracle page, User Dashboard, and Powerpool Vaults.
  • We completely reworked the xCVP page according to the new design.
  • We fixed an issue where changing the network in MetaMask caused the dApp to fall into an infinite loop of network changes.
  • We fixed an issue where changing the network in MetaMask caused the gas recommendations to come from the previous chain.
  • We fixed numerous issues that occurred when multiple Power Agents were on the same network.
  • We fixed an issue where the Job disable button wasn’t working.
  • We fixed an issue where the Resolver selector was set to 0x00000000 if a job was created in the UI.
  • We updated the network selector in the header.
  • We completely reworked the Pools and Farming pages in the deprecated products section.
  • We hide the explorer if there are no transactions on the selected network.
  • We fixed the issue that prevented withdrawing funds from the job owner.
  • We transferred all dApp requests to subQuery.
  • We updated the UI for the Applications page.
  • We changed the labels for Agent contracts on Arbitrum.
  • We implemented a mechanism to remove jobs from the blacklist upon any update, including config changes. Previously, jobs that were blacklisted remained in that state and did not start executing after becoming executable due to a config change without requiring container restart.
  • We developed a search feature on the application page of the dApp.

Cross-chain DCA trading strategy dApp

  • We started developing* the Cross-chain DCA trading strategy dApp using the core components of the current dApp.

UI/UX

  • We improved the menu structure in the current dApp.
  • We reworked the Applications page, Liquidity page, xCVP page, and all pages in the Deprecated Products section
  • We implemented a new design for wallet connection.
  • We designed the Cross-chain DCA trading strategy dApp for both desktop and mobile:

Subgraph

  • We deployed new subgraphs on GNOSIS, ARB, ETH, Polygon, Base.
  • We implemented* a check for data consistency between SubQuery and SubGraph.

subQuery

  • We added the BASE network to subQuery.
  • We added Ethereum, Sepolia, Polygon to subQuery.

Explorer

  • We added* BASE network support, implemented debugging, and fixed some errors.

*Some repositories are private. They will be opened in the future.

R&D development results from PowerPool

PowerAgent V2 testnet support

The research team continuously maintains the testnet. This includes monitoring the network, Keepers’ performance, and RPC infrastructure on various networks required for testing. We also communicate with testers, update testers’ leaderboards, and distribute weekly $CVP airdrops to top-performing Keepers [1][2][3][4].

Other testing activities and results (besides the routine testing and overall testnet maintenance mentioned above) delivered by the R&D team during the recent month:

  • We tested new versions of PowerAgent (0.5.7 and 0.5.8) on various chains
  • We tested the VRF operation
  • We reported 9 issues as a result of testing (Issue 81, Issue 82, Issue 83, Issue 84, Issue 85, Issue 86, Issue 87, Issue 88, Issue 89)

Research and product prototyping activities

  • We developed and deployed the Job for the Gearbox protocol (which automates gauge replenishment). Here is the Job and its description
  • We did research focused on launching products on BASE (top 20 Defi protocols to launch modified Limit order/DCA/Liquidation protection templates)
  • We did research focused on launching products on Arbitrum (top 20 Defi protocols to launch modified Limit order/DCA/Liquidation protection templates)
    -> All results will be published soon as an ecosystems overview article
    -> Using the research results, we created test Jobs modified specifically for Arbitrum/BASE DEX protocols
  • We worked on integrating Samudai points protocol, added all main PowerAgent activities for points count, continuously tested it, and provided technical requirements for other integrations
  • We researched the possibility of executing transactions using triggers produced by AI Agents, selected one protocol (POND), and drafted our view on how it could be automated by PowerPool
  • We contributed to the future PowerPool’s strategy and Proposal 65
  • We co-created the new PowerPool strategic vision and created an article describing it in detail (it will be published soon)
  • We created the Dune Dashboard for BASE (now it is used for testing; it will be public in the future)
  • We created the Dune Dashboard for monitoring VRF (now it is used for testing; it will be public in the future)

Results from PowerPool grantees

  • Partitura is ready to be added to PowerPool Apps. We tested Partitura DCA integration and provided bug reports; bugs were fixed.
  • SupremeDAO has launched its first automated yield strategy on the mainnet: Genesis! It simplifies the wstETH investment process for users while delivering superior and secure returns thanks to the efficient utilization of the PowerAgent dePin Keepers network.
  • Two grantee projects are finally ready to serve customers using PowerPool automation as an infrastructure

PowerPool at EthCC Brussels
On July 7th, Vasily Sumanov, PowerPool’s Head of Research, will be in Brussels to deliver a talk and participate in a panel discussion at the Hack Seasons.

During his speech, Vasily will discuss the current Web3 market challenges, and explain how PowerPool contributes to this evolving movement by providing the infrastructure for automated solutions in the AI and DeFi space.

If you are at EthCC this week and wish to discuss a possible collaboration, send a DM on X to arrange a meeting.

Other

  1. In collaboration with Binance Academy, PowerPool launched the “What is PowerPool (CVP)’’ Learn and Earn course. Users can now learn about PowerPool’s dePIN PowerAgent network and how it can benefit them and the ecosystem as a whole while simultaneously earning rewards!
  2. We participated in ETH Belgrade, met Gearbox, Mighty (an educational app for developers), and other friends
  3. PowerPool has joined a new vibrant community platform — Orb Club. Follow us on Orb Club to stay updated on all things PowerPool!
